reference.source: DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer / NCCN genetic/familial guidelines
clinicalPearls: Caused by germline pathogenic variants in a DNA mismatch-repair gene (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2) or by EPCAM deletions silencing MSH2, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern
The dominant risk is colorectal cancer, characteristically right-sided and early-onset, together with endometrial cancer as the leading extracolonic tumour in women
The wider spectrum includes ovarian, gastric, small-bowel, urothelial, hepatobiliary, pancreatic and brain tumours, with risk varying by the gene involved
Tumours typically show microsatellite instability and loss of mismatch-repair protein expression on immunohistochemistry, which guides germline testing
MLH1 promoter methylation and BRAF testing help distinguish sporadic microsatellite-unstable tumours from true Lynch syndrome
Regular colonoscopic surveillance with polyp removal substantially reduces colorectal cancer incidence and mortality
Amsterdam II and revised Bethesda criteria, alongside universal tumour screening, identify individuals who should proceed to germline testing
reference.pathophysiology: The syndrome stems from a germline defect in the DNA mismatch-repair system, which normally corrects base-base mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops that arise during replication. When the remaining functional allele is lost in a somatic cell, repair fails and errors accumulate, most conspicuously in repetitive microsatellite sequences, producing the microsatellite instability that characterises these tumours. The resulting hypermutable state generates numerous mutations in growth-regulatory genes, accelerating carcinogenesis and also creating neoantigens that make the tumours responsive to immune checkpoint blockade.
additionalDifferentials: Familial adenomatous polyposis and attenuated variants
Familial colorectal cancer type X without mismatch-repair deficiency
Sporadic microsatellite-unstable cancer due to MLH1 promoter methylation
additionalInvestigations: Tumour testing with mismatch-repair immunohistochemistry and microsatellite instability analysis
MLH1 promoter methylation and BRAF V600E testing to exclude sporadic causes when MLH1 is lost
Germline sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis of mismatch-repair genes and EPCAM
Gynaecological assessment including endometrial evaluation in women
Consideration of upper gastrointestinal and urinary tract surveillance based on the affected gene and family history
redFlags: Early-onset or right-sided colorectal cancer, particularly with mismatch-repair-deficient histology
Synchronous or metachronous Lynch-spectrum tumours in one individual
Postmenopausal or unexplained abnormal uterine bleeding in a carrier suggesting endometrial cancer
Painless haematuria in a carrier raising concern for urothelial malignancy
reference.prognosis: Cancer risk is high but gene-dependent, being greatest for MLH1 and MSH2 and lower for MSH6 and PMS2. Colonoscopic surveillance markedly reduces colorectal cancer mortality, and mismatch-repair-deficient tumours often respond well to immune checkpoint inhibitors, so outcomes are frequently favourable when the diagnosis is recognised.
pitfalls: Labelling a microsatellite-unstable tumour as Lynch syndrome without excluding MLH1 promoter methylation
Relying solely on family history criteria and missing carriers who do not meet Amsterdam or Bethesda thresholds
Overlooking endometrial and other extracolonic risks by focusing only on the colon
Failing to arrange cascade testing of relatives once a germline variant is confirmed
references: DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer: Principles and Practice of Oncology
NCCN Guidelines: Genetic/Familial High-Risk Assessment - Colorectal
management: Regular colonoscopy with polypectomy is the backbone of colorectal cancer risk reduction in Lynch syndrome carriers
Aspirin chemoprevention is supported by trial evidence specific to Lynch syndrome and is reasonable for routine use in carriers
When colorectal cancer arises in a carrier, extended rather than segmental colectomy is favoured given the ongoing risk of a second colon cancer
Women with Lynch syndrome carry a high lifetime endometrial cancer risk that varies by the specific mismatch-repair gene affected, and a meaningful ovarian cancer risk as well
Risk-reducing total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is recommended once childbearing is complete, timed before the expected age of natural menopause

Carriers considering risk-reducing gynaecologic surgery need dedicated counselling and support for sexual side effects such as vaginal dryness and decreased arousal, separate from the surgery's oncologic benefit
Prophylactic gynaecologic surgical specimens should be processed carefully with serial sectioning and peritoneal washings to detect occult malignancy

Established mismatch-repair-deficient, microsatellite-instability-high tumours resist adjuvant fluoropyrimidine-based chemotherapy and respond better to immune checkpoint inhibition with PD-1 blockade, favouring immunotherapy over conventional adjuvant chemotherapy
This dMMR immunotherapy-responsiveness principle is generally extended to other Lynch-spectrum cancers such as endometrial, gastric, and urothelial tumours as standard oncology practice
Patients under age 60 to 65 presenting with upper tract urothelial cancer, or with a suggestive personal or family cancer history, should be evaluated for Lynch syndrome
Gene- and family-history-directed surveillance of the upper gastrointestinal and urinary tracts is reasonable in carriers
Refer to a clinical geneticist for germline confirmation and cascade testing of relatives once a pathogenic variant is identified
A suspicious symptom in a Lynch-spectrum organ should prompt organ-specific work-up rather than reassurance based on a single recent negative surveillance test
Refer to gynaecologic oncology when a woman with Lynch syndrome is considering or approaching the age for risk-reducing hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy
